title: Exam & Tutorial Topic Framework Suggestions
text:
This document compiles real-world domain frameworks for designing future written exam questions and flipped lab tutorial tasks in Mathe3. Each domain pairs a feature variable (\(x\)) with a target response (\(y\)) while aligning with core linear algebra and machine learning concepts.






Feature Variable (\(x\)): Preparation Duration / Study Hours (\(x\), in hours).
Target Variable (\(y\)): Achieved Exam Score (\(y\), in points or %).
Model Equation: \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\)
Interpretation: \(\theta_0\) represents baseline knowledge (zero preparation), while \(\theta_1\) represents performance gain per study hour.
Exam Application: Standard, highly relatable baseline for \(2 \times 2\) matrix inversion, determinant checks, and parameter estimation.





Feature Variable (\(x\)): Text Document Length / Word Count (\(x\), in thousands of words).
Target Variable (\(y\)): Stylometric Vocabulary Richness / Unique Terms (\(y\), in count).
Model Equation: \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\)
Interpretation: \(\theta_0\) represents core vocabulary size, while \(\theta_1\) represents lexical expansion rate per 1,000 words.
Exam Application: Text mining and natural language processing context. Can be extended to term-document matrices or TF-IDF vector spaces.





Feature Variable (\(x\)): Inscription Weathering / Surface Age (\(x\), in centuries).
Target Variable (\(y\)): Optical Character Recognition (OCR) Accuracy (\(y\), in %).
Model Equation: \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\)
Interpretation: \(\theta_0\) represents unweathered inscription legibility, while \(\theta_1 < 0\) represents decay loss per century.
Exam Application: Digital heritage preservation context. Ideal for overdetermined systems showing noisy decay measurements.





Feature Variable (\(x\)): Door-to-Door Canvassing / Campaign Effort (\(x\), in hours per district).
Target Variable (\(y\)): Voter Turnout Rate (\(y\), in %).
Model Equation: \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\)
Interpretation: \(\theta_0\) represents baseline turnout without active campaigning, while \(\theta_1\) represents voter mobilization gain per campaign hour.
Exam Application: Social science and public policy context. Excellent for testing linear independence and multi-variable regression.





Feature Variable (\(x\)): Exhibition Duration (\(x\), in days).
Target Variable (\(y\)): Total Ticket Revenue (\(y\), in thousands of €).
Model Equation: \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\)
Interpretation: \(\theta_0\) represents opening-day advance sales, while \(\theta_1\) represents daily visitor revenue rate.
Exam Application: Applied economics context for fitting straight lines and calculating parameter vectors via \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{y}\).





Feature Variable (\(x\)): Audio Sampling Frequency (\(x\), in kHz).
Target Variable (\(y\)): Reconstructed Signal Fidelity / SNR (\(y\), in dB).
Model Equation: \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\)
Interpretation: \(\theta_0\) represents base signal noise floor, while \(\theta_1\) represents fidelity improvement per kHz.
Exam Application: Signal processing and engineering context. Good for demonstrating degenerate systems when two sample rates yield identical measurements.

title: Dictionary: Maths to NumPy
text:
Linear Algebra Concept
Mathematical Formula
NumPy / Python Implementation




Feature Vector
\(\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N]^T \in \mathbb{R}^N\)
x = np.array([20.0, 50.0])


Dot Product
\(\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^N x_i y_i\)
np.dot(x, y) or x @ y


Vector Norm (Length)
\(\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum x_i^2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}}\)
np.linalg.norm(x)


Angle between Vectors
\(\cos(\theta) = \frac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 \|\mathbf{y}\|_2}\)
np.dot(x, y) / (np.linalg.norm(x) * np.linalg.norm(y))


Design Matrix Construction
\(\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{x}] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 2}\)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(N), x])


Matrix-Vector Product
\(\mathbf{y}_{\text{pred}} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\)
y_pred = X @ theta


Determinant (\(2 \times 2\))
\(\det(\mathbf{X}) = ad - bc\)
np.linalg.det(X)


Matrix Trace
\(\text{tr}(\mathbf{X}) = \sum_{i=1}^N X_{ii}\)
np.trace(X)


Matrix Inverse (\(2 \times 2\))
\(\mathbf{X}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}\)
np.linalg.inv(X)


Linear System Solution
\(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{X}^{-1} \mathbf{y}\)
theta = np.linalg.solve(X, y)

\(\text{rank}(\mathbf{X})\)
np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)

title: Feature Engineering
text:
Feature engineering encompasses the mathematical preprocessing steps applied to raw features prior to fitting a statistical model. While raw observational data directly capture physical or clinical phenomena in their native measurement units, they frequently present challenges: disparate numerical scales, extreme skews, heavy tails, and heteroscedasticity.
Two fundamental classes of preprocessing address these challenges in distinct ways:
Setup and Data Load
import os
import sys
import numpy as np

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_theme(context="notebook", style="whitegrid")
FIGSIZE = (10, 8.5)

# Filter physiologically valid observations and standardize column names
valid = (df["insu"] > 0) & (df["plas"] > 0)

title: Feature Engineering
text:
1. Transformations: Changing Shape
Nonlinear transformations alter the geometric shape of feature distributions. Crucially, transformations must be applied prior to standardization.

Mathematical Formulations

Square Root Transformation: \[x^\prime = \sqrt{x}\]
Logarithmic Transformation: \[x^\prime = \log\left(\frac{x}{u_0} + 1\right)\] where \(u_0\) represents the characteristic reference unit of the measurement (e.g., \(1\,\mu\text{U/ml}\) for insulin), rendering the argument dimensionless.



Why Transform?

Dampening Influential Outliers & Leverage: In linear regression, parameter estimates \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\) are highly sensitive to observations far from the mean in feature space (high leverage points). For right-skewed variables such as insulin, a few extreme observations can dominate the sum of squared residuals (\(RSS\)). The concave nature of \(\log(x)\) compresses extreme values, pulling outliers closer to the median and stabilizing parameter estimates.
Stabilizing Variance (Homoscedasticity): Standard linear regression assumes constant residual variance across all values of the predictor: \(\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_i \mid x_i) = \sigma^2\). For Poisson-like count processes (such as pregnancies), the variance scales proportionally with the mean: \(\mathrm{Var}(X) \propto \mathbb{E}[X]\). The variance-stabilizing transformation for a Poisson process is the square root: \[\mathrm{Var}(\sqrt{X}) \approx \frac{1}{4}\]
Linearizing Relationships: Many biological processes obey power-law or exponential kinetics (\(y \propto x^\alpha\)). Log-transforming the variables converts multiplicative relationships into additive, linear equations amenable to ordinary least squares: \[\log(y) = \log(c) + \alpha \log(x)\]



Why Not Transform Everything?
Transformations should not be applied arbitrarily across all features:

Symmetric Physiological Variables: Variables such as blood_pressure, glucose, skin_thickness, and bmi are already relatively symmetric around biological setpoints. Applying a concave logarithmic transform to an already symmetric distribution creates an artificial negative (left) skew, degrading model fit.
Interval Variables & Demographic Metrics: Features like age have a uniform physical and epidemiological interpretation (e.g., risk change per year of age). Transforming age compresses the elderly age groups relative to young adults, distorting demographic comparability. The positive skew in age simply reflects the recruited cohort (younger adults in this study) rather than an unconstrained physical process.

title: Feature Engineering
text:
2. Normalization & Standardization: Changing Scale
Standardization rescales variables to a common numerical range without altering the relative distances between percentiles or the underlying distributional shape.

Mathematical Formulation
The standard score (\(z\)-score) is defined as:
\[z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]
where \(\mu = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) is the sample mean and \(\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2}\) is the sample standard deviation.


Affine Invariance & Properties

Affine Linear Transformation: Standardization is strictly an affine linear transformation of the form \(z = a x + b\), where \(a = 1/\sigma\) and \(b = -\mu/\sigma\).
Shape Invariance: Because affine mappings preserve ratios of lengths, standardization does not alter the skewness, kurtosis, or modality of the distribution. A skewed feature remains equally skewed after standardization; only its mean (\(0\)) and standard deviation (\(1\)) change.



Why Standardize?

Numerical Stability: When features differ by orders of magnitude (e.g., insulin in hundreds vs. pedigree in fractions of a unit), the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) can become ill-conditioned, leading to numerical errors when computing inverses. Centering and scaling maintains a well-conditioned matrix.
Preserving Sample Distances: Distance metrics such as the Euclidean distance: \[d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^p (x_{ik} - x_{jk})^2}\] are dominated by whichever feature has the largest raw numerical variance. Standardization ensures each feature contributes proportionally to geometric distances in clustering (k-means), nearest neighbors (k-NN), and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
Optimization & Regularization: In gradient descent, disparate feature scales cause the loss surface to take the form of elongated, eccentric ellipsoids, forcing optimization trajectories to oscillate inefficiently. Standardization produces circular/spherical level sets, allowing gradient updates to point directly toward the minimum. Furthermore, regularized loss functions (such as Ridge \(\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2\) and Lasso \(\lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_1\)) apply an isotropic penalty to coefficients; unstandardized features would result in arbitrary, unfair penalization dictated entirely by measurement units.

title: Feature Engineering
text:
3. Comparison Across Preprocessing Stages
The three-panel violin plot below illustrates the progressive impact of targeted preprocessing on the physiological features of the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset:

Raw, Unscaled Features: Dynamic ranges vary dramatically across native clinical measurement units (insulin reaches nearly 800, while pedigree remains below 2.5).
Standardized Features (\(z\)-scores): All eight features share zero mean and unit variance, making distributions comparable on a shared scale, but skews remain unchanged.
Targeted Transformations & Standardized Features: Targeted transformations are applied only where mathematically and clinically justified: square root for count-based pregnancies and logarithmic for heavy-tailed insulin. Naturally symmetric features (blood_pressure, glucose, skin_thickness, bmi, pedigree, age) are left untransformed, and all features are then standardized to \(z\)-scores.



Code
# Stage 1: Raw features
df_raw = df_clean[feature_cols]

# Stage 2: Standardized features (affine transform: preserves shape)
df_z = (df_raw - df_raw.mean()) / df_raw.std()

# Stage 3: Targeted shape transformations, followed by standardization
df_targeted = df_raw.copy()
# Variance stabilization for Poisson count process
df_targeted["pregnancies"] = np.sqrt(df_targeted["pregnancies"])
# Outlier compression for heavy-tailed biological concentration
df_targeted["insulin"] = np.log1p(df_targeted["insulin"])
# Other features (glucose, blood_pressure, skin_thickness, bmi, pedigree, age) remain untransformed

df_targeted_z = (df_targeted - df_targeted.mean()) / df_targeted.std()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 8.5))

# Panel 1: Raw Unscaled Features
sns.violinplot(data=df_raw, ax=axes[0], palette="Set2", cut=0, inner="quartile")
axes[0].set_title("Raw features, unscaled", fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Clinical Units")

# Panel 2: Standardized Features (z-score)
sns.violinplot(data=df_z, ax=axes[1], palette="Set2", cut=0, inner="quartile")
axes[1].set_title("Standardized features (z-score)", fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)
axes[1].set_ylabel("$z$-score")
axes[1].set_ylim(-4.5, 6.5)

# Panel 3: Targeted Transformations & Standardized Features
sns.violinplot(data=df_targeted_z, ax=axes[2], palette="Set2", cut=0, inner="quartile")
axes[2].set_title("Transformations (sqrt for pregnancies, log for insulin) + Standardizations", fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)
axes[2].set_ylabel("$z$-score")
axes[2].set_ylim(-4.5, 6.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: Comparison of preprocessing stages: raw clinical measurements (top), standardized features (middle), and targeted transformations (square root for count-based pregnancies, logarithm for heavy-tailed insulin) followed by standardization (bottom).











NoteKey Insights: Targeted Transformations, Nondimensionalization, and Power Transforms




Targeted Selection vs. Arbitrary Transformation: Transformations should be a targeted, domain-motivated choice rather than an automated default. Variables that are already relatively symmetric around biological setpoints (blood_pressure, glucose, skin_thickness, bmi) do not benefit from logarithmic compression; transforming them introduces an unnecessary negative skew. Similarly, interval variables such as age preserve chronological and epidemiological meaning in their linear form.
Requirement for Dimensionless Numbers: Mathematical transcendental functions (such as logarithms and exponentials) are rigorously defined only on pure, dimensionless numbers. When transforming a dimensionful physical measurement \(x\) with unit \([x]\) (e.g., serum insulin in \(\mu\text{U/ml}\)), division by a reference unit \(u_0 = 1\,[x]\) renders the quantity dimensionless (\(x^\prime = x / u_0\)) before applying \(\log(x^\prime + 1)\).
Generalized Power Transformations (Box-Cox): Many non-linear transformations belong to parameterized families. In particular, the Box-Cox Power Transformation generalizes power and logarithmic transforms for positive variables: \[y^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \frac{y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 0 \\ \ln(y) & \text{if } \lambda = 0 \end{cases}\] The parameter \(\lambda\) smoothly bridges between square root (\(\lambda = 0.5\)), natural logarithm (\(\lambda \to 0\)), and an untransformed linear shift (\(\lambda = 1\)). While automated optimization of \(\lambda\) can be useful in exploratory modeling, targeted transformations based on physical and biological principles remain the foundation of interpretable feature engineering.










CautionCautious Note: Parameter Interpretation with Preprocessed Features



Interpreting regression coefficients (slopes \(\theta_1\) and intercepts \(\theta_0\)) in original physical or clinical units requires reversing any applied transformations and standardizations:

Standardized Features: When \(x\) and \(y\) are standardized, the slope \(\beta_1\) represents a dimensionless effect size: the expected standard deviation change in \(y\) per standard deviation change in \(x\).
Log-Transformed Features: When \(x\) is log-transformed (\(x^\prime = \log x\)), the slope \(\theta_1\) measures relative elasticity: a 1% relative increase in \(x\) corresponds to an expected change of approximately \(0.01 \times \theta_1\) in \(y\).
Reversing Transformations: Before communicating predictive equations or baseline risks back to clinicians or decision-makers, model outputs must be mapped back to their original physical units (\(x = u_0(\exp(x^\prime) - 1)\)) to restore direct clinical interpretability.

Task 3: The Hat Matrix
Use basic numpy to:

Design Matrix: Calculate the design matrix.
Hat Matrix: Compute \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T\).
Equivalence Check: Verify that \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}\) is identical to model.predict(X).
Algebraic Properties: Verify that \(\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric, idempotent, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{H}) = p\).

Vector Construction: Construct vectors \(\mathbf{y}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), \(\bar{y}\mathbf{1}\), and residual \(\boldsymbol{e}\). Verify that \(\bar{y}\mathbf{1} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is orthogonal to \(\boldsymbol{e}\).
Pythagoras: Calculate the sums of squares and verify Pythagorean identity: \(TSS = ESS + RSS\).
Coefficient of Determination: Compute \(R^2\) and verify against scikit-learn.

title: 05 Linear Regression: Bias-Variance & Regularization
section: 1. The Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Concept & Formal Decomposition
text:
1. The Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Concept & Formal Decomposition
In Lecture 04, we witnessed the two opposing extremes of model flexibility:

Underfitting (High Bias): A rigid straight line (\(d = 1\)) fails to capture the underlying biological U-shaped curve, leaving non-random parabolic patterns in the residuals.
Overfitting (High Variance): A high-degree polynomial (\(d = 12\)) wiggles through every idiosyncrasy of the training data, exhibiting wild boundary oscillations, exploding parameter weights, and a near-singular Gram matrix.

How do we formalize this tradeoff mathematically?

1.1 The Visual Target: The Dartboard Analogy
To intuitively separate Bias from Variance, imagine firing arrows at a target bullseye. The center represents the true biological mechanism \(f(x)\), and each shot represents a model \(\hat{f}(x)\) trained on an independent random patient cohort \(\mathcal{D}_k\):


Generate 4-Panel Dartboard Target Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(10, 3.5))

np.random.seed(42)
n_shots = 20

configs = [
    ("Low Bias, Low Variance\n(Ideal Target)", 0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 'darkgreen'),
    ("High Bias, Low Variance\n(Underfitting: Rigid)", 0.9, 0.9, 0.2, 'crimson'),
    ("Low Bias, High Variance\n(Overfitting: Wild)", 0.0, 0.0, 0.7, 'darkorange'),
    ("High Bias, High Variance\n(Worst Case)", 0.9, 0.9, 0.7, 'darkred')
]

for ax, (title, mu_x, mu_y, spread, col) in zip(axes, configs):
    for r in [1.5, 1.0, 0.5, 0.15]:
        circle = plt.Circle((0, 0), r, color='gray' if r > 0.15 else 'gold', fill=(r == 0.15),
                            linestyle='-' if r > 0.15 else 'none', lw=1.2, alpha=0.3 if r > 0.15 else 0.8)
        ax.add_patch(circle)
    
    shots_x = np.random.normal(mu_x, spread, n_shots)
    shots_y = np.random.normal(mu_y, spread, n_shots)
    
    ax.scatter(shots_x, shots_y, color=col, s=25, edgecolors='black', lw=0.5, zorder=4)
    ax.scatter([0], [0], color='red', marker='+', s=70, lw=2, zorder=5)
    
    ax.set_xlim(-1.8, 1.8)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.8, 1.8)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: The Dartboard Analogy: Disentangling systematic error (Bias) from sample-to-sample volatility (Variance).






Bias: The distance between the average prediction \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]\) across cohorts and the true bullseye \(f(x)\).
Variance: How widely dispersed predictions \(\hat{f}(x)\) scatter around their own average.




1.2 Mathematical Derivation of the Bias-Variance Decomposition
Let us now derive why expected generalization error decomposes strictly into these two components plus irreducible noise.

Mathematical Setup:

True biological data-generating process: \(y = f(x) + \varepsilon\).
Measurement noise \(\varepsilon\) has mean \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\) and constant variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\).
Noise \(\varepsilon\) in a new test observation is independent of the model estimate \(\hat{f}(x)\) trained on historical data.

Let \(\hat{f}(x)\) be the model learned from a random training set \(\mathcal{D}\). Because \(\mathcal{D}\) is random, \(\hat{f}(x)\) is a random variable. Let \(\bar{f}(x) = \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]\) denote the expected model prediction averaged across all possible training cohorts.


Step 1: Expand the Expected Squared Prediction Error
\[\mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\left( (f(x) + \varepsilon) - \hat{f}(x) \right)^2\right]\]
Regroup into model error \((f(x) - \hat{f}(x))\) and noise \(\varepsilon\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\left( (f(x) - \hat{f}(x)) + \varepsilon \right)^2\right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] + 2\mathbb{E}[(f(x) - \hat{f}(x))\varepsilon] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]
\end{aligned}\]
Because \(\varepsilon\) is independent of \(\hat{f}(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\): \[\mathbb{E}[(f(x) - \hat{f}(x))\varepsilon] = \mathbb{E}[f(x) - \hat{f}(x)] \cdot \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\] \[\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2] = \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\]
Thus, total error separates into model error plus noise: \[\mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] + \sigma^2\]


Step 2: Decompose the Model Error
Add and subtract the expected prediction \(\bar{f}(x) = \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]\) inside the expectation:
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\left( (f(x) - \bar{f}(x)) + (\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}(x)) \right)^2\right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2\right] + 2\mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) - \bar{f}(x))(\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}(x))\right] + \mathbb{E}\left[(\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}(x))^2\right]
\end{aligned}\]
Notice that \((f(x) - \bar{f}(x))\) is a deterministic constant (independent of the training sample \(\mathcal{D}\)). Therefore: \[\mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) - \bar{f}(x))(\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}(x))\right] = (f(x) - \bar{f}(x)) \cdot \mathbb{E}[\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}(x)]\]
By definition of expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}(x)] = \bar{f}(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)] = 0\). The cross-term vanishes completely!


The Final Identity:
\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\right] = \underbrace{(f(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2}_{\text{Bias}^2(\hat{f}(x))} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[(\hat{f}(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2\right]}_{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{f}(x))} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{Irreducible Noise}}}\]






NoteThe Three Inescapable Error Components




\(\text{Bias}^2(\hat{f}(x))\): Systematic error from oversimplified assumptions (e.g., forcing a straight line onto curved biology).
\(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{f}(x))\): Model volatility across different patient cohorts (e.g., high-degree polynomials whose weights swing wildly).
\(\sigma^2\): Irreducible noise inherent to the biological system. No algorithm can ever predict below \(\sigma^2\).

title: 05 Linear Regression: Bias-Variance & Regularization
section: 2. Detecting Overfitting Empirically: Validation Splits & The U-Curve
text:
2. Detecting Overfitting Empirically: Validation Splits & The U-Curve
Because we never have access to the true data-generating function \(f(x)\) in practice, we cannot compute theoretical Bias or Variance directly. How do we detect whether our model is underfitting or overfitting?

2.1 The Golden Rule of Machine Learning
We split our available data into two independent sets: 1. Training Set (\(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\)): Used exclusively to estimate the parameter vector \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\). 2. Validation Set (\(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}\)): Held out during training and used exclusively to evaluate generalization performance.


Generate Empirical Validation U-Curve
np.random.seed(42)
n_total = 200
x_all = np.random.uniform(16.0, 45.0, n_total)
y_all = 2.0 + 0.040 * (x_all - 22.5)**2 + np.random.normal(0, 1.2, n_total)
y_all = np.clip(y_all, 0.5, None)

x_tr, x_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(x_all, y_all, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)

poly_range = list(range(1, 11))
train_losses = []
val_losses = []

for d in poly_range:
    model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(d), LinearRegression())
    model.fit(x_tr.reshape(-1, 1), y_tr)
    train_losses.append(np.mean((y_tr - model.predict(x_tr.reshape(-1, 1)))**2))
    val_losses.append(np.mean((y_val - model.predict(x_val.reshape(-1, 1)))**2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.5))
ax.plot(poly_range, train_losses, 'o-', color='#1f77b4', lw=2, label='Training Loss (MSE)')
ax.plot(poly_range, val_losses, 's--', color='crimson', lw=2.2, label='Validation Loss (MSE)')
ax.set_title('Model Complexity: Training vs. Validation Loss (The U-Curve)')
ax.set_xlabel('Polynomial Degree $d$')
ax.set_ylabel('Mean Squared Error')
ax.set_xticks(poly_range)
ax.set_ylim(0, 5)
ax.axvline(2, color='darkgreen', linestyle=':', lw=2, label='Optimal Complexity ($d=2$)')
ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=9)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: The Empirical Validation U-Curve: Training error drops monotonically with complexity, while validation error reaches a minimum and rebounds sharply.

title: 05 Linear Regression: Bias-Variance & Regularization
section: 3. \(L_2\) Ridge Regularization: Analytical Shrinkage & Invertibility Rescue
text:
3. \(L_2\) Ridge Regularization: Analytical Shrinkage & Invertibility Rescue
In Lecture 04, we discovered that as polynomial degree increases, two severe breakdowns occur: 1. Parameter weights explode to massive opposing magnitudes (\(\pm 10^6\)). 2. The Gram matrix determinant \(\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) \to 0\) collapses exponentially toward zero, making \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) practically or strictly non-invertible.
Rather than manually pruning features, Ridge Regression (\(L_2\) Regularization) adds a penalty on the squared Euclidean norm of the parameter vector to the cost function:
\[J_{\text{Ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2 = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta})^T(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda \boldsymbol{\theta}^T\boldsymbol{\theta}\]
where \(\lambda \ge 0\) is the regularization hyperparameter: * \(\lambda = 0\): Recovers standard Ordinary Least Squares. * \(\lambda \to \infty\): Drives all weights toward zero (\(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \to \mathbf{0}\)).

3.1 Analytical Derivation of the Ridge Normal Equations
Because the \(L_2\) penalty is quadratic and continuously differentiable everywhere, we can solve for \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{Ridge}}\) in closed form:

Expand the objective function: \[J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y} - 2\boldsymbol{\theta}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol{\theta}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} + \lambda \boldsymbol{\theta}^T\boldsymbol{\theta}\]
Take the vector gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\): \[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J = -2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + 2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} + 2\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}\]
Set the gradient to zero for optimality: \[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \lambda\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \implies (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]
Closed-form analytical solution: \[\boxed{\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{Ridge}} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}}\]



3.2 Rescuing the Collapsing Gram Matrix: The Eigenvalue Shift
Notice what adding \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) accomplishes algebraically:
In Lecture 04, we saw that as columns of \(\mathbf{X}\) become collinear, the smallest eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) plunge toward zero: \(\lambda_{\min} \to 0\).
If \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_i \ge 0\), then the regularized matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}\) has eigenvalues: \[\tilde{\lambda}_i = \lambda_i + \lambda \ge \lambda > 0 \qquad \text{for all } i\]
Its determinant is strictly positive: \[\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}) = \prod_{i=1}^p (\lambda_i + \lambda) \ge \lambda^p > 0\]
The Fundamental Mathematical Guarantee: For any \(\lambda > 0\), the regularized matrix \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\) is guaranteed to be strictly positive-definite and non-singular, even when \(p > n\) or when features are perfectly collinear! Ridge regression completely eliminates the numerical instability observed in Lecture 04.

title: 05 Linear Regression: Bias-Variance & Regularization
text:
4. \(L_1\) Lasso Regularization: Geometric Sparsity
While Ridge shrinks coefficients continuously toward zero, it never sets any weight exactly to zero.
Lasso Regression (\(L_1\) Regularization) replaces the squared \(L_2\) penalty with the sum of absolute values:
\[J_{\text{Lasso}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol{\theta})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\theta_j|\]
Because the absolute value function \(|\theta_j|\) is non-differentiable at \(\theta_j = 0\), Lasso has no closed-form solution and is solved numerically via coordinate descent.

4.1 The Geometric Diamond Argument
To understand why Lasso produces exact zeros (sparsity), consider the equivalent constrained optimization formulations:
\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \text{RSS}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \begin{cases} \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2 \le C & \text{(Ridge)} \\ \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_1 \le C & \text{(Lasso)} \end{cases}\]

Ridge (\(L_2\) Ball): The constraint boundary is a smooth sphere/circle. The elliptical contours of the RSS objective contact the circle at arbitrary smooth points, where neither coordinate is zero.
Lasso (\(L_1\) Diamond): The constraint boundary has sharp corners located precisely on the coordinate axes (\(\theta_1 = 0\) or \(\theta_2 = 0\)). An expanding elliptical RSS contour contacts these sharp corners first with high probability.

Thus, Lasso performs automatic feature selection, driving irrelevant or redundant feature weights strictly to zero!

When an applied machine learning model performs poorly on unseen test patients, what concrete action should an engineer take?
In Stanford CS229, Andrew Ng formalized a rigorous diagnostic methodology based on Learning Curves (plotting training and validation error as a function of training sample size \(m\)).

title: 02 Linear Regression: Model Spaces
text:
Model Spaces: Variables and Parameters
We distinguish between two complementary spaces:

Variable Space \((x, y)\): Each observation (e.g. patient) is a point \((x_i, y_i)\), and a candidate model is represented as a line \(\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\).
Parameter Space \((\theta_0, \theta_1)\): The space of model configurations. Each point \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_0, \theta_1)\) represents an entire candidate model. The loss function \(RSS(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) forms a convex quadratic bowl over this parameter plane.

Regression Goal: \[RSS(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}))^2 = \mathbf{e}^T \mathbf{e} \to \min\]
Parameterized Models: Each parameter combination \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_0, \theta_1)\) corresponds to a specific (linear) model in variable space.
Loss Topography: Some models have a lower loss; For a given dataset (\(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{y}\)), the OLS solution \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\) sits precisely at the unique global minimum.
Samples May Need Selection: Sometimes samples have to be removed because of missing or wrongly annotated data.
Variables May Need Transformations: In this first example, insulin and glucose are plotted in their raw, untransformed clinical units, but sometimes feature transformations (e.g. \(\tilde{x} = \log(x)\)) could improve model fit and stabilize variance. See the Feature Engineering reference guide.
Parameter Interpretation: Parameters may carry units and meaning; intercept \(\theta_0\) is the baseline level at zero input, and the slope \(\theta_1\) is the expected response rate per unit increase in the predictor.
Even the Best Models Will Be Wrong: No straight line can fully capture true biological complexity.









ImportantSummary




For a given dataset we can find the optimal linear model: unique & deterministic
Model still has uncertainties due to:

sampling variability: parameter estimates
irreducible noise: residuals
systematic bias: model misspecification

We previously analyzed paired observations of Carbohydrate Intake \(x\) (g) and Blood Glucose Response \(y\) (mg/dL) for \(n = 2\) patients using a system of linear equations:

An exact inverse \(X^{-1}\) exists, passing a line perfectly through both points with zero residual error.

2. The Gram Trick
What happens if we take the rectangular system \(y = X\theta\) and multiply both sides on the left by \(X^T\)?
\[y = X \theta \implies X^T y = X^T X \theta \implies \theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\]

Squaring the System: Multiplying \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{100 \times 2}\) by its transpose \(X^T \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 100}\) converts the rectangular system into a square, symmetric \(2 \times 2\) Gram matrix (\(X^T X\)).
The Pragmatic Solution: Assuming \(X^T X\) is invertible, left-multiplication by \(X^T\) immediately yields a concrete solution \(\theta\).







NoteWhat is the origin of this trick?




minimizing losses
maximizing likelihood
geometric projection

We define the Residual Sum of Squares \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\) as the squared \(L_2\) norm of the error vector \(e\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{RSS}(\theta) &= \|e\|^2 = e^T e = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 \\
&= (y - X\theta)^T (y - X\theta) \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad \text{minimize}
\end{aligned}\]
Notice that RSS is a simple number (a scalar product).



Deriving the OLS Estimator
To find the optimal parameter vector \(\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}}\), we minimize \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\) by setting its gradient to zero:






NoteStep-by-Step Derivation






Expand the Residual Sum of Squares \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\): \[\begin{aligned}
\text{RSS}(\theta) &= e^T e = (y - X\theta)^T (y - X\theta) \\
&= y^T y - y^T X \theta - \theta^T X^T y + \theta^T X^T X \theta \\
&= y^T y - 2 \theta^T X^T y + \theta^T X^T X \theta
\end{aligned}\]
Notice: \(y^T X \theta = \theta^T X^T y\) is a scalar.
Compute the gradient vector with respect to \(\theta\): \[\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta \text{RSS}(\theta) &= -2 X^T y + 2 X^T X \theta \\
&= -2 X^T (y - X\theta) = -2 X^T e
\end{aligned}\]
Notice: \(\text{RSS}(\theta)\) is a scalar and the gradient \(\nabla_\theta \text{RSS}(\theta)\) has the same dimensions as \(\theta\)
Set the gradient to zero (First-Order Necessary Condition): \[-2 X^T e = 0 \iff X^T X \theta = X^T y \quad \text{(Normal Equations)}\]
Solve for \(\theta\) assuming \(C = X^T X\) is invertible: \[\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} = C^{-1} X^T y \quad \text{where } C = X^T X\]
Dimensions Summary: \[\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}, \quad C = X^T X \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, \quad C^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, \quad X^T \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times n}, \quad y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\]
Notice: for our motivating example \(n=100\) and \(p=2\)




\[\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\]

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
4. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

Probabilistic Modeling of Noise
\[y_i = x_i^T \theta + e_i\]
Assume residual errors \(e_i\) are independent Gaussian noise: \[e_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \implies y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(x_i^T \theta, \sigma^2)\]



The Likelihood Function \(L(\theta)\)
Assuming the model is correct, the probability of a single observation \(y_i\) is:
\[p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)\]
Assuming independent observations, the joint likelihood of observing all \(n\) patient responses is the product over all observations:
\[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)\]



Maximizing Log-Likelihood
Taking the natural log turns the product into a sum:
\[\ell(\theta) = \ln L(\theta) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2\]
Maximizing \(\ell(\theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\):
\[\arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta) \iff \arg\min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i^T\theta)^2 = \arg\min_\theta \|y - X\theta\|^2\]

Takeaway: Under Gaussian noise, Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) yields the exact same estimator as OLS!

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
5. Geometric Derivation
Instead of calculus, we can derive OLS purely using Linear Algebra & Vector Projections in observation space (\(\mathbb{R}^n\)):

Observation Space (\(\mathbb{R}^n\)): The target vector \(y \in \mathbb{R}^n\) lives in \(n\)-dimensional observation space (\(n=100\)). The origin \(\mathbf{0}\) represents zero response for all patients.
Model Subspace (\(\text{col}(X)\)): All possible predictions \(\hat{y}\) are linear combinations of the columns of \(X\): \[\begin{bmatrix} \hat{y}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}_n \end{bmatrix} = \theta_0 \mathbf{1}_n + \theta_1 \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{bmatrix}\] where \(\mathbf{1}_n\) denotes the \(n \times 1\) column vector of ones. All possible parameter combinations \((\theta_0, \theta_1)\) trace out the column space \(\text{col}(X)\), and any model prediction \(\hat{y}\) is simply an element of this subspace.
Orthogonal Projection: The point \(\hat{y} \in \text{col}(X)\) closest to \(y\) is the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto \(\text{col}(X)\).




Geometric Projection View of OLS




Orthogonality Condition
The residual error vector \(e = y - \hat{y} = y - X\hat{\theta}\) must drop at a right angle (\(\perp\)) onto \(\text{col}(X)\):
\[e \perp \text{col}(X) \iff X^T e = 0\]
Substituting \(e = y - X\hat{\theta}\):
\[X^T (y - X\hat{\theta}) = 0 \implies X^T y - X^T X \hat{\theta} = 0 \implies X^T X \hat{\theta} = X^T y\]

Conclusion: Both Calculus (\(\nabla_\theta \text{RSS} = 0\)) and Geometry (\(e \perp \text{col}(X)\)) yield the exact same Normal Equations!

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
6. Model Predictions
With the optimal parameters \(\hat \theta\), we can compute predicted responses \(\hat{y}\) for any patient data \(X\):
\[\hat{y} = X\hat{\theta} = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T y = H y \quad \text{where } H = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T\]

The Hat Matrix (\(H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\)): \(H\) transforms observed responses \(y\) directly into fitted predictions \(\hat{y}\) (“putting a hat on \(y\)”).
Projection Operator: The hat matrix \(H\) is symmetric (\(H^T = H\)) and acts as a projection operator that maps any vector from observation space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) onto the model subspace \(\text{col}(X)\), as illustrated in the geometric projection figure.

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
7. History of Regression
Behind every mathematical formula are historical pioneers, contextual motivations, and critical ethical reflections:



Historical Pioneers of Ordinary Least Squares: Carl Friedrich Gauss, Francis Galton, and Karl Pearson








WarningHistory and Ethics of Statistics




The Controversial Legacy: Both Francis Galton (who coined the term “eugenics”) and Karl Pearson (who held the Galton Chair of Eugenics at UCL) developed foundational statistical tools to quantify human genetics and social hierarchies.
Modern Data Science Lesson: Mathematics and algorithms are formal structures, but data selection, feature choice, and modeling goals are never strictly neutral. Understanding bias in statistical data is essential for responsible Machine Learning.

title: 01 Linear Regression: Introduction
text:
8. Summary

Matrix power: \(y = X\theta\)
Modesty: \(y = X\theta + e\)
Optimism:

\(e^T e \to \mbox{min}\)
\(e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\)
\(e \perp \hat{y}\)

Solution: \(\hat \theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\)
Predictions: \(\hat y = X \hat \theta\)
Projections: \(\hat y = H y\), where \(H = X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T\) is the hat matrix: \(H = H^T = H^2\).

import urllib.request
import json

# Helper function to render DataFrame head as a clean Markdown table
def df_to_markdown(dataframe):
    cols = list(dataframe.columns)
    header = "| " + " | ".join(cols) + " |\n| " + " | ".join([":---:"] * len(cols)) + " |\n"
    rows = "\n".join("| " + " | ".join(f"{val:.4f}" if isinstance(val, float) else str(val) for val in row) + " |" for row in dataframe.values)
    return header + rows



1. Celestial Mechanics: Data from NASA
To explore how data measurements behave in physical systems, we analyze real long-term observational ephemeris data of the planet Mars tracked over a 125-year timeline (1900–2025) obtained from the NASA JPL Horizons API.
Astronomers track planetary motions using three primary observables:

Right Ascension (RA): Celestial longitude measured in hours (\(0\) to \(24\text{ h}\)).
Declination (Dec): Celestial latitude measured in degrees (\(-26.5^\circ\) to \(+26.5^\circ\)).
Apparent Magnitude (Magnitude): Observed luminosity on an inverse logarithmic brightness scale.



Read Data
# Query NASA JPL Horizons API for Mars (Body 499) observed from Earth (500@399) over 125 years (1900-2025)
url = ("https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api?"
       "format=json&COMMAND='499'&CENTER='500@399'&MAKE_EPHEM='YES'"
       "&EPHEM_TYPE='OBSERVER'&START_TIME='1900-01-01'&STOP_TIME='2025-01-01'"
       "&STEP_SIZE='14d'&QUANTITIES='1,9'")

req = urllib.request.urlopen(url)
data = json.loads(req.read().decode('utf-8'))
result_text = data['result']




Process Data
# Parse ephemeris records between $$SOE (Start of Ephemeris) and $$EOE (End of Ephemeris)
start_idx = result_text.find('$$SOE') + 6
end_idx = result_text.find('$$EOE')
lines = result_text[start_idx:end_idx].strip().split('\n')

records = []
for line in lines:
    parts = line.strip().split()
    if len(parts) >= 9:
        # Convert sexagesimal RA (hours, minutes, seconds) to decimal hours [0, 24)
        ra_h = float(parts[2]) + float(parts[3])/60.0 + float(parts[4])/3600.0
        
        # Convert sexagesimal Dec (degrees, arcminutes, arcseconds) to signed decimal degrees [-90, +90]
        dec_deg_val = float(parts[5])
        sign = -1.0 if parts[5].startswith('-') else 1.0
        dec_deg = dec_deg_val + sign * (float(parts[6])/60.0 + float(parts[7])/3600.0)
        
        try:
            mag = float(parts[8])
        except (ValueError, IndexError):
            mag = None
        records.append({'DateStr': parts[0], 'Date': pd.to_datetime(parts[0]), 'RA': ra_h, 'Dec': dec_deg, 'Magnitude': mag})

# Primary baseline dataset `df` loaded from real NASA JPL Horizons observational data
df = pd.DataFrame(records)

2. Planetary Models and Simulation
In addition to real empirical data, we can build a mathematical model of planetary orbits. Simplified models (such as assuming a circular orbit with constant velocity) capture fundamental behaviors (parallactic retrograde loops, declination bounds, and opposition brightness flares), but miss subtle physical effects like Keplerian speed variations near aphelion.
The code block below generates a 2,000-year synthetic dataset stored in DataFrame df_sim:


Simulate Data
# 1. Parameter setup (2,000 years * 52.1775 weeks = 104,355 data points)
np.random.seed(1337)
jahre = 2000
wochen_pro_jahr = 52.1775
n_points = int(jahre * wochen_pro_jahr)

# Time axis (in years)
t = np.linspace(0, jahre, n_points)

# --- Variable 1: Right Ascension (RA) ---
# Simplified circular orbit assumption (constant orbital speed)
ra = np.mod(t * (1.0 / 1.8808) * 24, 24)
ra = np.mod(ra + np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) * 0.8, 24)

# --- Variable 2: Declination (Dec) ---
dec = 26.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t + np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 1.8808) * 0.1)

# --- Variable 3: Apparent Magnitude ---
synodisch = np.mod(t, 2.135)
distanz_effekt = np.exp(-((synodisch - 1.07) / 0.12)**2)
exzentrizitaet = 1.0 + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 15.0)

magnitude = 1.75 - (3.85 * distanz_effekt * exzentrizitaet)
magnitude = np.clip(magnitude, -2.94, 1.86)

# Construct synthetic DataFrame `df_sim`
df_sim = pd.DataFrame({
    'RA': ra,
    'Dec': dec,
    'Magnitude': magnitude
})

We examine the density distributions of each observable using Kernel Density Estimates (KDE).


Visual Summaries Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 4.0))

sns.kdeplot(df['RA'], fill=True, bw_adjust=1.2, color='darkcyan', ax=axes[0])

# Plot 3: Magnitude Density (Skewed)
sns.kdeplot(df['Magnitude'], fill=True, bw_adjust=0.5, color='darkorange', ax=axes[2])

3.2 Numerical Summaries
Following visual inspection, we compute standard numerical summary statistics (df.describe() and sample variance) rendered programmatically as a structured table.


Numerical Summaries Table

desc = df_num.describe()

for stat_key, stat_label, fmt in metrics_map:

4. Interpretations

4.1 Right Ascension (RA)

RA spans \([0, 24)\) hours across the celestial sphere.
In real observational data (df), RA exhibits a pronounced accumulation peak around \(\sim 11.5\text{ h}\).
The position of this peak corresponds to Aphelion (where Mars moves slowest in its orbit according to Kepler’s Second Law, spending more time per degree).







NoteDetailed Analysis of Right Ascension & Real Physics vs. Circular Models






Real Physics (Keplerian Aphelion Slowdown): Real Mars has an eccentric orbit (\(e \approx 0.0934\)). Its Aphelion (farthest point from the Sun) is located at ecliptic longitude \(\sim 154^\circ\), corresponding to \(\text{RA} \approx 11\text{ h} - 12\text{ h}\) (constellation Leo/Virgo). According to Kepler’s Second Law (Equal Areas in Equal Times), Mars travels slowest near Aphelion (\(v \approx 21.9\text{ km/s}\)) and fastest near Perihelion (\(v \approx 26.5\text{ km/s}\)). Mars spends \(\sim 20\%\) more time per orbit lingering near Aphelion, creating a real physical accumulation peak around \(\text{RA} \sim 11.5\text{ h}\) in df.
Circular Model Assumption: A simplified circular generator uses constant velocity \(\text{ra} = \frac{24}{1.8808} t + \text{parallax}\). Because speed is held constant, the underlying distribution of a circular model is perfectly uniform across \([0, 24)\text{ h}\).
Circular Topology: RA represents directional angles on the celestial sphere (\(0.0\text{ h}\) and \(23.99\text{ h}\) are physically adjacent). Standard linear summary statistics treat them as opposite extremes, rendering linear means (\(\approx 11.65\text{ h}\)) misleading without directional/circular statistics.






4.2 Declination (Dec)

Dec exhibits a strongly bimodal (U-shaped) distribution, with twin peaks concentrated near the extrema of \(\pm 26.5^\circ\).
The mean (\(\approx +1.20^\circ\)) and median (\(\approx +2.37^\circ\)) point directly to the location of minimum observed data density.
Origin of the \(\pm 26.5^\circ\) Extrema: The declination boundaries are determined by Earth’s axial tilt (\(23.44^\circ\)) plus Mars’ orbital inclination (\(1.85^\circ\)) relative to the ecliptic plane, causing Mars’ celestial latitude to oscillate smoothly between \(-26.5^\circ\) and \(+26.5^\circ\).







NoteDetailed Analysis of Declination






Harmonic Dwell Time: Because harmonic motion slows down near maximum amplitudes (\(\frac{d}{dt}\sin(\omega t) \to 0\)), Mars lingers near its northern and southern turning points (\(\pm 26.5^\circ\)) and rushes through the celestial equator (\(0^\circ\)).
Failure of Unimodal Metrics: Summary statistics like mean and variance assume a single central cluster. Reporting \(\mu = 1.20^\circ\) and \(\sigma = 17.26^\circ\) makes the dataset sound like a bell curve centered at \(0^\circ\), completely masking the twin peaks at the boundaries.






4.3 Apparent Magnitude (Magnitude)

Highly asymmetric distribution with a dominant baseline peak near faint magnitudes (\(+1.1\text{ to }+1.8\) mag) and a long left tail extending to bright magnitudes (down to \(-2.95\) mag during opposition flares).
The mean (\(0.70\) mag) is distorted by rare opposition flares and is not very meaningful (giving a magnitude at which Mars is almost never observed). Baseline visual faintness dominates the quantiles (where larger numerical magnitude values denote dimmer visual brightness).







NoteDetailed Analysis of Apparent Magnitude






Distortion by Rare Events: For ~90% of its synodic cycle, Mars is far from Earth and faint. During brief opposition alignments, brightness flares up. The mean (\(0.70\) mag) is pulled away from the true baseline mode by these rare flares, giving an average value at which Mars is almost never observed.
Quantile Collapse: Because baseline faintness dominates, interquartile range (\(IQR\)) collapses, hiding the extreme flare range down to \(-2.95\) mag during perihelic oppositions.








5. Takeaways and Skepticism

Beware the Gaussian Default: Introductory courses heavily rely on Normal distribution assumptions (\(\mu, \sigma^2\)). As planetary movements demonstrate, physical processes frequently produce uniform, bimodal, and long-tailed distributions where standard means and variances fail to describe the data.
Summary Tables Condense, But Also Conceal: Aggregating data points into 8 numbers per variable collapses critical spatial and modal structures (such as bimodal peaks in Dec or opposition spikes in Magnitude).
Always Look at the Data (EDA First): Visual inspection (histograms and KDE density plots) must precede numerical summary calculations. Visual plots immediately reveal multi-modality, skewness, boundary effects, and circular topologies.
Context & Domain Expertise Matter: Observables are physical measurements over time. Understanding planetary orbits (Kepler’s laws, retrogrades, synodic cycles, aphelion slowing) explains why distributions take their specific shapes. Note also domain conventions: in astronomy, magnitude is an inverted logarithmic scale where larger numbers represent dimmer objects, and lower/negative numbers represent brighter objects.
Beware of Data Scales, Units, and Transformations:

Variables within the same dataset often use completely different units and scales: RA in hours (\(0–24\text{ h}\)), Dec in degrees (\(-90^\circ\) to \(+90^\circ\)), and Magnitude on an inverted logarithmic scale.
Transforming, standardizing, or normalizing data (e.g. z-score standardization or min-max scaling) requires careful attention to domain units and physical topologies before applying standard algorithms blindly.

Beware of Visualization Artifacts:

Analysts must carefully distinguish between model assumptions, physical mechanisms, and smoothing artifacts.
Density estimation algorithms can introduce boundary smoothing effects (such as KDE edge leaks), whereas physical drivers (like Keplerian velocity variations near aphelion) produce genuine non-uniform data structures. Visual inspection must always be paired with physical domain understanding.

title: 03 Linear Regression: Uncertainties
text:
Parameter Uncertainties
Sampling fluctuations (measured by \(\sigma^2\)) induce uncertainty in the parameter estimates \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\):
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}
\]
\[
\sigma^2 \approx \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{RSS}{n - p}
\]






NoteMathematical Derivation: Parameter Covariance





A model is a mapping from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{y}\). \[
\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{x}) + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}
\] In general, \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) captures both systematic errors (e.g. model misspecification) and irreducible measurement errors.
Let’s assume \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) contains only independent, homoscedastic measurement errors for \(n\) observations (samples): \[
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n
\]
For linear regression, the OLS parameter vector \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) can be obtained as a linear mapping of the target vector \(\mathbf{y}\): \[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{y} \qquad \text{where } \mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times n}
\] Applying the bilinear property of covariance: \[
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{A} \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{A}^T
\] This reduces to: \[
\mathbf{A} (\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n) \mathbf{A}^T = \sigma^2 \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}
\]
We estimate the unknown scalar observation variance \(\sigma^2\) from the sample residuals \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\): \[
\sigma^2 \approx \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\mathbf{e}^T \mathbf{e}}{n - p} = \frac{RSS}{n - p}
\]





Parameter Covariance Matrix Heatmap
# 1. Construct design matrix including intercept column of ones
X_design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
n, p = X_design.shape

# 2. Residual variance estimate sigma^2_hat
residuals = y - model.predict(x)
sigma2_hat = np.sum(residuals**2) / (n - p)

# 3. Covariance matrix: Cov(theta_hat) = sigma2_hat * (X^T X)^(-1)
gram_inv = np.linalg.inv(X_design.T @ X_design)
cov = sigma2_hat * gram_inv

param_labels = [r"$\theta_0$ (Intercept)", r"$\theta_1$ (Slope)"]
cov_df = pd.DataFrame(cov, index=param_labels, columns=param_labels)


# Visual Heatmap of the Covariance Matrix
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(
    cov_df,
    annot=True,
    fmt=".4g",
    cmap="RdBu_r",
    center=0,
    cbar_kws={'label': 'Covariance'},
    ax=ax
)
ax.set_title(r"Parameter Covariance: $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$", fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()





Diagonal Elements: Variance of each parameter (\(SE(\hat{\theta}_j)^2\)). Off-Diagonal Elements: Covariance between parameters (\(\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\theta}_j, \hat{\theta}_k)\)).




We can quantify parameter uncertainty using a confidence interval:
\[
\hat{\theta}_j \pm c \cdot SE(\hat{\theta}_j)
\]
The multiplier \(c\) is arbitrary and corresponds to the desired confidence level (\(c=1.96\) for a 95% interval under standard normal approximation, or \(t_{n-p, 1-\alpha/2}\) under the Student’s \(t\)-distribution).


Parameter Uncertainty Summary
# Standard errors and parameter correlation
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
print("Parameter Uncertainty Summary:")
print(f"  Residual Variance (sigma^2): {sigma2_hat:.4f}")
print(f"  Residual Std Error (sigma):  {np.sqrt(sigma2_hat):.4f} mg/dL")
print(f"  Intercept theta_0:          {intercept:.4f} +/- {se[0]:.4f} (SE)")
print(f"  Slope theta_1:              {slope:.4f} +/- {se[1]:.4f} (SE)")

Model Uncertainties

Residual Analysis
In general, we would expect that the inclusion of additional predictors (e.g. insulin) would reduce the residual errors compared to the baseline (mean) model.


Code

jitter = rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, size=len(y))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=FIGSIZE)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Data in \(n\) Dimensions



Geometric Decomposition in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): \(\mathbf{y} = \bar{y}\mathbf{1} + (\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}) + (\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}})\)


We can express the data vector \(\mathbf{y}\) as a step-by-step progression:

Base Model (The Mean): \(\bar{\mathbf{y}} = \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\), the horizontal benchmark where no input features are used.
Improved Model (The Linear Fit): Moving from the base model \(\bar{y}\mathbf{1}\) to the full prediction \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) captures the improvement provided by the input features.
Observation Error: Moving from the prediction \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) to the actual observation \(\mathbf{y}\) represents the remaining unexplained error.

In vector notation: \[
\mathbf{y} = \underbrace{\bar{y}\mathbf{1}}_{\text{Base model}} + \underbrace{(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1})}_{\text{Explained improvement}} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}})}_{\text{Unexplained error}}
\]
Subtracting the baseline mean vector \(\bar{y}\mathbf{1}\) from both sides centers the decomposition around the null model:
\[
\underbrace{(\mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1})}_{\text{Total deviation}} = \underbrace{(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1})}_{\text{Explained deviation}} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}})}_{\text{Residual deviation}}
\]

Pythagoras in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
Recall that OLS minimizes \(\|\mathbf{e}\|^2\) by projecting \(\mathbf{y}\) orthogonally onto the model column space \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\). The residual vector \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is perpendicular to every column in \(\mathbf{X}\):
\[
\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = \mathbf{0}
\]
Because both \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) and the vector \(\mathbf{1}\) lie in \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\), their difference \((\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1})\) also lies entirely in \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\). Consequently:
\[
(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1})^T (\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = 0
\]
The explained vector and the residual vector meet at a right angle in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
Applying the Pythagorean Theorem to this right triangle:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|^2 &= \|\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2 \\ \\
TSS &= ESS + RSS \\ \\
(n - 1) &= (p - 1) + (n - p)
\end{aligned}
\]










Component
Vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
Sum of Squares Formula
df
Mean Square\(MS = SS / df\)




Total(\(TSS\))
\(\mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\)
\(n - 1\)
\(s_y^2 = \frac{TSS}{n - 1}\)


Explained(\(ESS\))
\(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\)
\(p - 1\)
\(MS_{\text{exp}} = \frac{ESS}{p - 1}\)


Residual(\(RSS\))
\(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\)
\(n - p\)
\(MS_{\text{res}} = \frac{RSS}{n - p} = \hat{\sigma}^2\)




Total Degrees of Freedom (\(n - 1\)): The observation vector \(\mathbf{y}\) lives in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Subtracting the sample mean imposes \(1\) linear constraint (\(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y}) = 0\)), leaving \(n - 1\) independent directions of variation.
Explained Degrees of Freedom (\(p - 1\)): The model subspace \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\) has dimension \(p\). Because the constant intercept baseline already occupies \(1\) dimension (\(\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{1})\)), the remaining \(p - 1\) slope features add \(p - 1\) independent degrees of freedom (\(1\) dof for simple linear regression).
Residual Degrees of Freedom (\(n - p\)): The OLS normal equations force the residuals to be strictly orthogonal to all \(p\) columns of \(\mathbf{X}\) (\(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}\)). These \(p\) linear constraints confine the residual vector to the orthogonal complement subspace \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})^\perp\) of dimension \(n - p\).




Fraction of Explained Variation (\(R^2\))
The Coefficient of Determination (\(R^2\)) measures the proportion of total variation in \(y\) successfully explained by the linear model:
\[
R^2 = \frac{ESS}{TSS} = 1 - \frac{RSS}{TSS} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}
\]
\(R^2\) also relates to the angle \(\phi\) of triangle \(\triangle(\bar{y}\mathbf{1}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \mathbf{y})\) at vertex \(\bar{y}\mathbf{1}\): \[
\cos(\phi) = \frac{\|\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|}{\|\mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|} = \sqrt{\frac{ESS}{TSS}} \implies \cos^2(\phi) = R^2
\]

If the model explains all variability (\(RSS = 0\)): \[ESS = TSS \implies R^2 = 1 \to \phi = 0^\circ\]
If the model performs no better than the constant mean (\(ESS = 0\)): \[RSS = TSS \implies R^2 = 0 \to \phi = 90^\circ\]




Relative Improvement by the Model (\(F\)-statistic)
To assess the relative improvement achieved by the model (\(ESS = TSS - RSS\)), we compare the explained sum of squares (\(ESS\)) to the unexplained residual noise variance (\(RSS\)).
Since both quantities have different degrees of freedom we divide each term by its respective degrees of freedom to compare Mean Squares. This ratio is called the \(F\)-statistics:
\[
F = \frac{MS_{\text{exp}}}{MS_{\text{res}}} = \frac{ESS / (p - 1)}{RSS / (n - p)}
\]
A large \(F\)-statistic (\(F > 1\)) indicates large improvements over the baseline model.

title: 03 Linear Regression: Uncertainties
text:
Prediction Uncertainties
Uncertainties in model parameters directly propagate into uncertainties in model predictions.

Confidence Intervals
For a new input query, we define the column vector \(\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, x_{\text{new}})^T\) containing the constant \(1\) for the intercept and the predictor value \(x_{\text{new}}\).
The leverage (or variance multiplier) for \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is given by:
\[
h(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{x}_0^T (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_0 = \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_{\text{new}} - \bar{x})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]






NoteConnection to the Full Hat Matrix \(\mathbf{H}\)



The leverage scalar \(h(\mathbf{x}_0)\) quantifies how far any input \(\mathbf{x}_0\) lies from the center of the training data. For an in-sample observation \(\mathbf{x}_i\), \(h(\mathbf{x}_i) = H_{ii}\) is precisely the \(i\)-th diagonal element of the full \(n \times n\) Hat Matrix: \[\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \qquad ( \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y})\] Diagonal elements \(H_{ii} \in [1/n, 1]\) measure how strongly observation \(y_i\) influences its own fitted prediction \(\hat{y}_i\).


Confidence interval for the expected response \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}_0]\):
\[
\hat{y}(\mathbf{x}_0) \pm t_{n-p, 1-\alpha/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{h(\mathbf{x}_0)}
\]


Python Implementation
# Make predictions on training data with confidence interval
X_pred = x
y_pred = model.predict(X_pred)

n = len(y) # observations
p = X_pred.shape[1] + 1 # parameters (2)

# Calculate residuals and standard error
eps = y - y_pred
sig = np.sqrt(np.sum(eps**2) / (n - p))

# Calculate confidence interval (82% level)
confidence_level = 0.82
t_val = stats.t.ppf((1 + confidence_level) / 2, n - p)
h = 1/n + (X_pred - X_pred.mean())**2 / np.sum((X_pred - X_pred.mean())**2)
se = sig * np.sqrt(h)

lwr = y_pred - t_val * se
upr = y_pred + t_val * se

# Display first few predictions
pred_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'insulin': X_pred.flatten()[:5],
    'fit': y_pred.flatten()[:5],
    'lwr': lwr.flatten()[:5],
    'upr': upr.flatten()[:5]
})

Prediction Intervals
The variation of individual patient observations is clearly larger than suggested by the confidence interval shown above.
It is important to remember that in our linear model there are two distinct components of variation:
\[
\|\mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2 + \|\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|^2
\]

Variance explained by the linear model: \(\|\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\|^2\) where \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X} \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\). Errors in parameter estimation induce uncertainty in the estimated mean \(\hat{y}_0\).
Unexplained observation noise: \(\|\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2 = \|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\|^2\), where each individual patient exhibits natural physiological deviation \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\).

To capture where a new individual patient’s measurement will fall, we must include both parameter uncertainty and individual measurement noise:
\[
h(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{x}_0^T (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_0
\]
\[
\hat{y}(\mathbf{x}_0) \pm t_{n-p, 1-\alpha/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{1 + h(\mathbf{x}_0)}
\]


Python Implementation
# Prediction intervals with full variability
prediction_level = 0.82
t_val_pi = stats.t.ppf((1 + prediction_level) / 2, n - p)

# Prediction interval includes both model uncertainty (h) and residual variance (1)
se_pi = sig * np.sqrt(1 + h)

lwr_pi = y_pred - t_val_pi * se_pi
upr_pi = y_pred + t_val_pi * se_pi

plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

NoteNotice



The prediction interval covers the broader scatter of future individual observations. Even with infinite data (\(n \to \infty, h \to 0\)), the prediction interval never collapses to zero because irreducible physiological noise \(\sigma\) remains.

plt.figure(figsize=FIGSIZE)

# Plot training data
plt.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.4, color='#1f77b4', label="Observed Data")

# Plot extrapolated fit and prediction intervals
plt.plot(X_extrap, y_extrap, 'r-', linewidth=2, label="Model Fit")
plt.fill_between(
    X_extrap.flatten(),
    lwr_extrap.flatten(),
    upr_extrap.flatten(),
    alpha=0.2,
    color='red',
    label=f"{int(prediction_level*100)}% PI"
)

# Reference lines for physical domain boundaries
plt.axvline(0, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7, label="Zero Insulin")
plt.axhline(0, color='black', linestyle=':', alpha=0.5, label="Zero Glucose")

plt.xlabel('Serum Insulin [µU/ml]')
plt.ylabel('Blood Glucose [mg/dL]')
plt.legend(loc='upper left')
plt.title("Models are ignorant.")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()









Linear models are agnostic to domain realities: they merely summarize (compress) the observed data within the training range and should not be used far outside the domain in which they were fitted. The model is completely ignorant of what negative serum insulin (or negative glucose level) means.


Preparing for Multivariate Analysis
In general, models have multi-variate predictors \(\mathbf{X}\). In such cases it is impossible to plot target \(y\) against all inputs simultaneously. Instead, it is standard practice to plot observed target \(y\) against the predicted values \(\hat{y}\):


Python Implementation
plt.figure(figsize=FIGSIZE)
plt.scatter(y_pred, y, alpha=0.4, color='#1f77b4', label="Data") 

plt.plot(yp, yp, 'r-', linewidth=2, label='Ideal Fit ($y = \hat{y}$)')
plt.fill_between(yp, yl, yu, alpha=0.2, color='red', label=f'{int(prediction_level*100)}% PI')
plt.xlabel('Predicted Glucose $\hat{y}$ [mg/dL]')
plt.ylabel('Observed Glucose $y$ [mg/dL]')
plt.legend()
plt.title(f'Observed vs. Predicted with Prediction Interval {prediction_level:.2f}')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

1. Categorical Inputs & One-Hot Encoding
Linear regression is not restricted to continuous numerical measurements. Real-world medical datasets regularly record qualitative (categorical) attributes—such as biological sex, smoking status, or blood type.
To include a categorical attribute with \(K\) distinct categories \(c_1, \dots, c_K\) in a linear model, we map each qualitative level to a binary indicator variable (dummy column):
\[d_{ki} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if observation } i \text{ belongs to category } c_k \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Consider the Medical Cost Personal Dataset (from Tutorial 02b), which records patient age, biological sex, and annual medical charges:

If we construct indicator columns for both sexes (\(\mathbf{d}_{\text{female}}\) and \(\mathbf{d}_{\text{male}}\)) alongside an explicit intercept column \(\mathbf{1}\), their row-wise sum is identically equal to the intercept column:
\[\mathbf{d}_{\text{female}} + \mathbf{d}_{\text{male}} = \mathbf{1}\]
This creates an exact linear dependency among the columns of \(\mathbf{X}\). The rank of \(\mathbf{X}\) is strictly less than the number of columns \(p\), making the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) singular (non-invertible).
